title: AI as a Workflow Partner
goal: Leave a manager listening with the feeling that this is approachable and already within reach - that it starts with one unglamorous task rather than a transformation, that it does not require being technical, and that the parts of the job they care about stay theirs.
audience: Managers in any field who suspect they are behind on this and are slightly embarrassed about it.
house_rules: Open on the week, not on the technology. If the first question contains the word AI, the listener braces.
Push every abstract answer down to one task. A platform is not a story; 'I stopped writing the Friday roll-up' is.
Take the honest limits beat seriously. An unqualified pitch costs you the audience's trust for everything after it.
Never ask how to make a team feel supported - it produces a change-management answer. Ask what the team actually said.
Approachable does not mean uncritical. It means the listener finishes thinking 'I could try that on Monday' rather than 'I am already too far behind.'

anchoring.$comment: The four flavors of every beat, ordered by how much they presuppose about the guest's current situation. This is the axis that makes an arc survive a guest whose circumstances turned out to be different from what you were told.
anchoring.current: Assumes they are in the seat right now and can speak freely about it. Most vivid, most fragile - it breaks if they have left, are between roles, or cannot discuss a current employer.
anchoring.experience: Draws on their own history without requiring a current employer. Still personal and specific. The safe default when you are not certain, and the flavor to reach for mid-interview when something surprises you.
anchoring.observed: About what they have watched others do. Works for consultants, vendors, advisors, and anyone who has just moved on. Requires no personal exposure at all.
anchoring.general: Principle only. Works even when the guest cannot discuss any specifics for legal or professional reasons. Least vivid - do not run a whole episode here.

beats.title: The recognizable week
beats.purpose: Ground the episode in a working reality before any technology enters it, so the audience meets a peer rather than an evangelist.
beats.listener_payoff: Recognition. They hear their own week described by someone else.
beats.keep_it_approachable: No mention of AI in this question at all. The whole beat exists to establish that the guest has the same week the listener does.

flavors.current: Walk me through last week. Where did the time actually go?
flavors.experience: Think about a week when you were closest to the work. Where did the time actually go?
flavors.observed: When you sit down with managers and map out their week, where does the time actually go?
flavors.general: What does a manager's week actually consist of, once you strip out what the job description says?

followups: How much of that was the work, and how much was moving the work along?
Which part of that would you hand to someone else tomorrow if you could?
beats.if_it_stalls: Pick one day. Tuesday. Start at the beginning of it.

beats.title: The first thing that stuck
beats.purpose: The concrete small win. This is the single most important beat for approachability - one unglamorous task, handed over, and kept.
beats.listener_payoff: A specific first move they could picture themselves making.
beats.keep_it_approachable: Push until the answer is one task. If you get a platform, a strategy, or a maturity model, ask again. The distinction between 'tried' and 'never took back' is what separates real adoption from experimentation.

flavors.current: What is the first thing you handed over and never took back?
flavors.experience: What was the first thing you handed over that actually stuck?
flavors.observed: When this works for someone, what is the thing that tends to stick?
flavors.general: What is the first thing that usually sticks - not the first thing people try, the first thing that lasts?

followups: How long before you stopped double-checking it?
What did you try before that, that did not stick?
beats.if_it_stalls: Not the impressive one. The boring one you would be slightly embarrassed to admit.

beats.title: How technical do you actually have to be
beats.purpose: Remove the perceived prerequisite. A large share of the audience has quietly disqualified themselves on the grounds that they are not technical.
beats.keep_it_approachable: If the guest is unusually technical, ask them to answer for someone who is not. Otherwise this beat backfires and confirms the listener's fear.

flavors.current: How technical do you actually have to be to do what you are doing?
flavors.experience: How technical did you have to become? What did you never learn and never needed?
flavors.observed: Are the people getting the most out of this the technical ones, or is it something else?
flavors.general: What does someone actually need to understand, and what can they safely ignore?

followups: What is the thing people think they need to learn that they do not?
Who on a team usually turns out to be good at this? Is it who you would expect?
beats.if_it_stalls: Say I am a manager with no technical background at all. What is genuinely out of reach for me, and what is not?

beats.title: From errand to partner
beats.purpose: Move the audience from picturing a window they go to ask things, to something living inside the work. The central reframe of the episode.
beats.listener_payoff: The conceptual shift, delivered in physical terms rather than abstract ones.
beats.keep_it_approachable: The word 'partner' can sound like marketing. Ground it in where the thing physically lives - a separate window they open, or the tool they already had.

flavors.current: Is it something you go to, or something already inside the tools you work in? What changed when that changed?
flavors.experience: Did it move from being somewhere you went to something that was just there? What changed when it did?
flavors.observed: For the teams you watch, has it moved out of the chat window into the tools? What changes when it does?
flavors.general: What is the real difference between AI you go and ask, and AI that is already sitting in the workflow?

followups: Which of the two produces better work?
What is still stuck in a chat window that should not be?
beats.if_it_stalls: Where does it physically live for you - a browser tab, or inside the {work_unit} you already had open?

beats.title: Where it falls down
beats.purpose: Honesty, which is what makes everything else credible. An unqualified pitch loses the room.
beats.listener_payoff: Permission to be skeptical - which, counterintuitively, lowers the barrier to trying it.
beats.keep_it_approachable: Ask for specifics inside their domain, not general AI criticism. 'It makes things up' helps nobody. 'It cannot read our older records' is useful.

flavors.current: Where does it fall down in your work, specifically?
flavors.experience: Where did it consistently fall down in the work you know best?
flavors.observed: Where do you watch it fall down most often?
flavors.general: What is it reliably bad at, in this kind of work?

followups: Did you work around it, or stop using it there entirely?
How long did it take you to find that out?
beats.if_it_stalls: What did you have to stop trusting it with?

beats.title: What stays yours
beats.purpose: Reassurance and identity. Naming what remains theirs makes the whole subject feel like addition rather than subtraction.
beats.listener_payoff: The job is not disappearing, and here is the part that is theirs.
beats.keep_it_approachable: This is the beat that speaks to the anxious listener. Ask it warmly and let the answer breathe - do not rush to the next question.

flavors.current: What is the part of your job you would not hand over, even if it worked perfectly?
flavors.experience: What was the part you never handed over?
flavors.observed: What do the managers you work with hold onto, even once they could delegate it?
flavors.general: What should stay with a person, even when the tool could do it?

followups: Is that a judgment, or a preference?
Has that line moved in the last year? Which direction?
beats.if_it_stalls: What would you feel wrong about automating, even if nobody would ever know?

beats.title: Knowing when to check
beats.purpose: Name the genuinely new skill - deciding what to verify - without making it sound like an extra burden.
beats.listener_payoff: A practical method, and permission to stop checking everything.
beats.keep_it_approachable: Frame it as a skill they already have from managing people, not a new discipline they have to acquire.

flavors.current: How do you decide when to check the work and when to let it go?
flavors.experience: How did you work out when to check and when to let it go?
flavors.observed: How do people get calibrated on when to check the work?
flavors.general: How should someone decide what to verify and what to trust?

followups: What did it take before you stopped checking everything?
Has anything gotten past you? What happened?
beats.if_it_stalls: Is it the same instinct you use with a new person on the team, or a different one?

beats.title: What the team actually said
beats.purpose: The people beat, asked for observed reality rather than best practice.
beats.listener_payoff: A realistic preview of the conversation they are quietly dreading.
beats.keep_it_approachable: Do not ask how to make a team feel supported - that phrasing contains its own answer and produces a change-management response. Ask what people actually said, including the unflattering parts.

flavors.current: When you brought this to your team, what did they actually say?
flavors.experience: When you brought this to a team, what did they actually say?
flavors.observed: When a manager brings this to a team, what do people actually say?
flavors.general: What does a team actually say when this arrives - not what the engagement survey says?

followups: Who was most resistant, and were they wrong?
Did anyone ask you about their job? What did you tell them?
beats.if_it_stalls: What was the first objection, in the first meeting?

beats.title: Where the work piled up instead
beats.purpose: Turn a tool conversation into a process conversation. One step got faster and the queue moved somewhere.
beats.listener_payoff: The insight that makes them look at their whole workflow rather than at a tool.
beats.keep_it_approachable: This is the most structural beat in the arc. Keep it concrete - a named step, a named queue, a named person - or it drifts into consulting language.

flavors.current: Once one step got faster, where did the work pile up instead?
flavors.experience: When one step got faster, where did the work pile up?
flavors.observed: When a team speeds up one step, where does the queue reappear?
flavors.general: If one step in a process gets dramatically faster, what usually happens to the rest of it?

followups: Is the new bottleneck a person?
Did anyone plan for that, or did you discover it the hard way?
beats.if_it_stalls: Who is waiting on whom now, that was not waiting before?

beats.title: Monday morning
beats.purpose: The takeaway close. One thing to try, and one thing not to start with.
beats.listener_payoff: A first step, and protection against the failure that would make them give up.
beats.keep_it_approachable: Insist on both halves. The 'do not start with' half is what stops a listener failing on their first attempt and concluding it is not for them.

flavors.current: A manager listening wants to try one thing this week. Based on what is working for you now, what should it be - and what should they not start with?
flavors.experience: Based on what actually worked for you, what should someone try first - and what should they not start with?
flavors.observed: Based on what you have watched succeed and fail, what should someone try first - and what should they not start with?
flavors.general: What should someone try first, and what should they not start with?

followups: How long before they should expect it to feel worth it?
What should they do if the first attempt is disappointing?
beats.if_it_stalls: Name the specific task. Not the category - the task.
